name: GraphQL N+1 and DataLoader
intent: Understand why a GraphQL query resolved field by field turns into 1 + N + N*M backend calls, how DataLoader batching collapses them, and how to stop a single query from costing too much.
scenario: A client asks for 50 posts, each with its author and its 20 comments, and each comment with its author. Resolved naively that is 1 + 50 + 50 + 1,000 = 1,101 database queries for one HTTP request; with DataLoader it is 4.
problem: A GraphQL query is a tree, and the server executes it by calling one resolver per field per parent object. A resolver for Post.author does not know that 49 sibling resolvers are about to ask for other users, so each one issues its own SELECT. The cost grows with the shape of the data and the shape of the query, both chosen by the caller, so the same endpoint can take 5 ms or 5 seconds, and a hostile client can pick the expensive shape on purpose.

howItWorks.title: The executor walks the tree, one resolver per field per object
howItWorks.text: For { posts { author { name } } } the executor runs Query.posts once, then Post.author once for every post it returned. Each resolver sees one parent and cannot see its siblings, so the natural implementation is one lookup per call: 1 query for the list plus N for the nested field. Nest a list inside the list and it becomes 1 + N + N*M. ORMs do the same with lazy loading (post.author inside a loop), and REST does it when a client fetches a list and then GET /users/{id} for each item. The pattern is the cost model, not a GraphQL bug.

howItWorks.title: DataLoader collects keys during one tick, then fires one batch
howItWorks.text: A loader exposes load(key) and returns a promise. It does not query immediately: it queues the key and schedules a dispatch for the end of the current tick of the event loop (process.nextTick or a microtask, after all the resolvers of the same level have run). At dispatch it calls your batch function once with every key, for example SELECT * FROM users WHERE id IN (3, 7, 12, ...), and resolves each promise with its own row. Your batch function must return results in the same order and length as the keys, using null or an error for a missing key.

howItWorks.title: Batching and caching are two different mechanisms
howItWorks.text: Batching merges different keys requested in the same tick into one query. Caching (memoization) returns the same promise for the same key requested again. DataLoader does both by default, but they save different things: with 1,000 comments written by 40 people the cache turns 1,000 key lookups into at most 40, while batching is what turns those 40 separate queries into 1. The cache lives in a loader created per request, never at module level, otherwise one user's data is served to another and stale rows live forever.

howItWorks.title: Levels are still sequential, so latency is depth, not N
howItWorks.text: Post.author and Post.comments are resolved in the same tick, so their loaders batch independently and run in parallel. Comment.author needs the comments first, so it waits for the next tick. The query above therefore costs 3 sequential database rounds regardless of N and M. Batching cannot remove depth, which is why a root-level JOIN can still win on round trips when the shape is fixed, at the price of coupling the resolver to the query and returning wide, repetitive rows.

howItWorks.title: Cost model for defence: count what the query can ask for
howItWorks.text: The same multiplication that causes N+1 is the denial-of-service lever. Aliases repeat a field 50 times at depth 1, cyclic relations (post { comments { post { comments ... } } }) nest as deep as the caller likes, and first: 100000 asks for a huge page. Defences stack: validate depth, estimate cost from the page sizes and per-field weights before executing (GitHub caps first/last at 100 and a call at 500,000 nodes), accept only persisted or allow-listed queries from first-party clients, put a timeout and a rate limit on the operation, and cap pagination on every connection.

howItWorks.title: Measure per field, because the average hides it
howItWorks.text: A slow request does not say which resolver is guilty. Record the latency and call count of each resolver (Apollo tracing, OpenTelemetry spans per field, or sampled traces) and watch two numbers: queries per request and the p99 of the slowest field. A field that runs 1,000 times per request with a 3 ms query is a 3 second request even though every individual query looks fast in the database dashboard.

pros: Backend calls drop from 1 + N + N*M to one per level of the tree, independent of list sizes
The fix lives in the data-access layer; resolvers stay small and composable, and the client does not change
The per-request cache also removes duplicate lookups, such as the same author on many comments
Cost analysis and persisted queries turn an unbounded public query language into a bounded API
cons: Latency is still proportional to query depth: each level waits for the one before it
One IN query with thousands of keys can be slower than a few smaller ones and may hit parameter limits
Loaders must be created per request and keyed carefully; a shared loader leaks data across users and stale rows
Batching hides the problem from the database but not from your process: a 442,050-object response still costs CPU and memory
Cost estimation is approximate: it relies on page sizes and weights that must be kept in sync with the schema
whenToUse: Any GraphQL resolver that fetches a related object per parent (author, owner, category, count)
Services where the same resolver is called many times per request through nested lists
Public or partner GraphQL endpoints where callers can write arbitrary queries
ORM-backed code with lazy relations that is slow only on list pages
whenNotToUse: Root fields that fetch one object or a handful: a loader adds machinery and saves nothing
When the relation can be fetched in the parent query for every client (a fixed screen): a join or a prefetch is simpler
As a replacement for cost limits: batching makes each query cheaper, not the allowed query smaller
Dependencies with no batch endpoint and no way to build one: you still make N calls, just concurrently, so bound the concurrency instead
pitfalls: A module-level loader: the cache never expires and one request can read another user's authorised data
A batch function that returns rows in database order instead of key order, or drops missing keys, so results are attached to the wrong parent
Calling load inside a loop after an await: keys land in different ticks and the batches degrade back toward one per key
Treating the cache as invalidation-free: after a mutation in the same request, a cached read returns the old object unless you clear or prime it
Depth limit only: 50 aliases of a depth-3 query pass it and cost 50 times more; cost analysis has to look at breadth and page sizes too
Limiting by timeout only: by the deadline the database has already done most of the work, and slow queries from many clients still queue behind each other
Unbounded first/limit arguments, or a connection with no default page size, so the cost estimate is whatever the client types
Monitoring only HTTP latency: without per-field timings and queries per request, an N+1 shows up only as a vague p99 regression

roles.label: Client
roles.description: Sends one GraphQL query describing a tree of data.

roles.label: GraphQL executor
roles.description: Walks the query tree and calls one resolver per field per parent object.

roles.label: DataLoader
roles.description: Collects the keys requested in one tick, batches them and caches per request.

roles.label: Database
roles.description: Answers each query with a base cost plus a cost per row.

roles.label: Query guard
roles.description: Rejects queries whose depth or estimated cost is over the limit before any resolver runs.
